ai-at-work.title: Meta AI director Rohit Patel leaves to take on Microsoft Office and Google Workspace
ai-at-work.excerpt: Rohit Patel is departing Meta after eight years working on AI evaluations and reinforcement learning, TechCrunch has exclusively learned. His startup, Ndoc, aims to take on Microsoft Office Suite.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Rohit Patel just walked away from Meta's AI shop to run Ndoc, a startup gunning for Microsoft Office and Google Workspace with AI smarts. This matters because the productivity software wars are heating up and talent is clearly voting with their feet toward the next big thing. After eight years at Meta, he's betting that AI-powered document tools can crack the market that's been Microsoft's fortress for three decades, which is either visionary or the kind of moonshot that keeps VCs awake at night.

ai-at-work.title: Opera introduces a new web standard to let users deploy AI locally in their browser
ai-at-work.excerpt: The new standard, WebAI, is designed to work with a variety of AI models.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Opera is pushing a new web standard called WebAI that lets users run AI models directly in their browsers instead of sending everything to the cloud. This matters because digital workplace teams are already scrambling to figure out privacy, security, and compliance around AI tools, and local processing could become a real alternative to cloud-dependent solutions. Honestly though, getting browsers to agree on anything is like herding cats wearing different colored collars, so whether WebAI actually becomes standard or just becomes another footnote in tech history remains to be seen.

ai-at-work.title: General Compute raises $100 million Series A, countering the neocloud disaster narrative
ai-at-work.excerpt: General Compute is betting on inference chips from outside the Nvidia ecosystem.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: General Compute just landed $100 million in Series A funding to build inference chips that don't depend on Nvidia's dominance. This matters because digital workplaces run on compute infrastructure, and chip diversification means potentially better availability and pricing for the AI tools your organization actually uses. Here's the thing though: another well-funded startup solving the chip problem is great, but it won't matter one bit if the software running on those chips is still a dumpster fire.

ai-at-work.title: Regal debuts Goal Oriented Agents, putting an actor and a director model on every call
ai-at-work.excerpt: Enterprise voice artificial intelligence company Regal Voice Inc. today added Goal Oriented Agents to its platform, enabling businesses using them to define what a call has to accomplish, and providin
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Regal Voice rolled out Goal Oriented Agents, a new AI feature that splits call handling between two models: one that acts and one that directs, letting businesses define what each call needs to accomplish. This matters because most digital workplace communication still happens on calls, and automating them with actual direction beats the usual chatbot that just flails around hoping something sticks. I've seen plenty of AI call tools that sound like they're reading from a fortune cookie, so splitting the work between an actor and director might actually produce something that doesn't make people want to hang up immediately.

tools-tech.title: Microsoft offers exits to thousands of employees, including staff on AI and Copilot teams
tools-tech.excerpt: Microsoft is offering voluntary exit packages to about 60,000 employees, roughly 27% of its workforce, including staff on teams building Copilot and other AI products, as the company looks for ways to
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft is offering voluntary exit packages to roughly 27% of its workforce (about 60,000 people) to fund AI investments, including some staff working on Copilot and related AI products. This matters because it signals that even the biggest tech companies are making hard choices about headcount and priorities, which could reshape how organizations think about their own digital workplace strategies and AI spending. Apparently the future of AI is so expensive that you've got to pay people to leave today, which is a pretty expensive way to fund innovation if you think about it.

tools-tech.title: OpenAI bets on AI economics with lower-cost GPT-6.1 Terra
tools-tech.excerpt: OpenAI has launched GPT-6.1 Terra, a new reasoning model that it says delivers near-frontier performance on visual reasoning, professional task execution, and computer-use benchmarks without the premi
tools-tech.dwp_take: OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra, a cheaper reasoning model designed to handle visual tasks, professional work, and automation without breaking the bank compared to their pricier models. For digital workplace teams, this matters because it finally makes serious AI capabilities accessible for enterprise automation projects that were previously cost-prohibitive. Here's the thing though: we've heard the "lower cost, same performance" story before, and I'll believe the real-world adoption numbers in six months when people stop running benchmarks and start running their actual messy business processes through it.

tools-tech.title: The right model at the right moment: Vendors push their agentic AI PC vision
tools-tech.excerpt: AI is getting expensive, and companies are looking to cut token costs. The solution: move more AI work to PCs. The PC won’t replace the cloud. Preliminary AI work can be done on a PC, and tougher work
tools-tech.dwp_take: Vendors are pushing the idea of running AI workloads locally on employee PCs instead of always routing them through expensive cloud services, with the PC handling lighter tasks and the cloud handling the heavy lifting. This matters because every dollar your company spends on token costs is a dollar not spent on actual productivity tools, and IT needs to understand this hybrid model to make smart infrastructure choices. The funny part is we're basically reinventing the mainframe versus desktop debate, except now we're calling it "agentic AI" and pretending it's revolutionary when it's really just economics finally catching up to common sense.

tools-tech.title: Microsoft Teams to get AI protection against phishing and fraud
tools-tech.excerpt: Microsoft is adding a new AI-powered security feature to Teams aimed at detecting phishing, scams, and identity theft by analyzing conversations, Bleeping Computer reports. Instead of primarily checki
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft is rolling out an AI feature in Teams that analyzes conversation patterns to spot phishing and fraud attempts rather than just scanning for malicious links. This matters because most security breaches still happen when someone clicks the wrong thing or trusts the wrong person, so catching suspicious behavior in real time actually addresses how attacks really work. Finally, someone at Microsoft remembered that the biggest security hole isn't the technology, it's the human sitting in front of it getting fooled by a convincing message.

digital-culture.title: At this point, 80% of job seekers apply and hear nothing
digital-culture.excerpt: In today’s hiring environment, job seekers are lucky to get rejected. In a recent survey by hiring platform Greenhouse, 81% of job seekers said they never heard back from a company, be it human or mac
digital-culture.dwp_take: Job seekers are getting ghosted by companies at alarming rates, with 81% experiencing radio silence after applying and nearly a third saying it happens constantly. This matters to digital workplace pros because your hiring tech and processes directly create this experience, and when candidates feel ignored, they're not coming back to your employer brand even if you eventually do hire them. After thirty years in this space, I can tell you that a bad applicant experience isn't just rude, it's expensive: those ghosted candidates are telling their networks your company doesn't respect their time, and word travels fast.

industry-news.title: Apple Unveils New iPad mini: What You Get for $699
industry-news.excerpt: Apple unveils a new iPad mini with OLED, A20 Pro and IP67 protection. See the $699 starting price, key specifications, release details and buyer advice. The post Apple Unveils New iPad mini: What You
industry-news.dwp_take: Apple released a refreshed iPad mini with OLED display, A20 Pro chip, and IP67 water resistance at a $699 starting price. For digital workplace folks, this matters because the iPad mini remains a legit productivity device for field workers, remote teams, and anyone who needs portable computing without going full laptop. Honestly, at this price point you're paying mostly for the Apple ecosystem and that shiny OLED screen, which is nice but won't revolutionize how your organization actually works.

industry-news.title: ChatGPT Custom GPT Retirement: How to Migrate Before Dec. 11
industry-news.excerpt: OpenAI is retiring custom GPTs in December. Here's what creators and Enterprise administrators need to know about deadlines, plugin migration, custom actions and sharing. The post ChatGPT Custom GPT R
industry-news.dwp_take: OpenAI is shutting down custom GPTs on December 11th and forcing users to migrate to a new system or lose their work. This matters because plenty of enterprises have built custom GPTs into their workflows as quick productivity shortcuts, and now IT teams have to scramble to move them before the deadline or rebuild from scratch. After thirty years watching platforms kill off features workers actually liked, I can tell you this is peak tech company behavior: launch something, get people dependent on it, then change the rules with a tight deadline.

industry-news.title: OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Terra Targets Workplace Automation at Lower Cost
industry-news.excerpt: OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Terra cuts standard API token prices by 50%. Explore its automation capabilities, availability and what IT teams should test before adoption. The post OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Terra Targets W
industry-news.dwp_take: OpenAI just dropped GPT-6.1 Terra with a 50 percent price cut on API tokens, making AI automation significantly cheaper for workplace applications. This matters because every digital workplace leader is scrambling to justify AI investments to the CFO, and suddenly the math gets a lot friendlier. Here's the thing though: cheaper tokens don't mean cheaper mistakes, so IT teams better have a solid testing plan or they'll be explaining why they automated the wrong process to the wrong stakeholders.

industry-news.excerpt: This eDegree covers Claude prompting, automation, integrations, and coding for practical business use. The post This $20 Claude AI Course Is Built for Work, Not Just Prompts appeared first on TechRepu
industry-news.dwp_take: Someone's selling a Claude AI course for twenty bucks that promises to teach actual work applications instead of just the "ask it anything" party trick version.
